III
Let us look once more at the disposition of these grumblers
in the parable. If anyone perchance asks: did they experience
God's goodness, did it not rather come to the men who were
hired last? the very question betrays a wrongness of outlook.
Is it not always a great and splendid thing to see God's
goodness in action? Should we not be ready to rejoice when-
ever we see a manifestation of God's generosity, whether it be
I myself or someone else who is its object? Yes, that is just
the point; are we able to feel joy in the good which comes to
others? For of course this capacity to rejoice with others is
the sign of a noble and kind disposition.
"Do you begrudge my generosity?" asks the householder
in the parable. Should not the surly fellow have been
ashamed as he realized that he ought to have been pleased
to think that his comrades were being so generously treated?
Instead of this his heart was filled with a petty envy when he
saw that another man was getting better treatment than
himself. And do we suppose that a heart like this could be
capable of perceiving God's sheer goodness when he himself
becomes the object of it? No! such a man will never be aware
of it, even when generous treatment is meted out to him, for
he will not be capable of confessing with shame: "Lord,
I am not in the least worthy of all the faithfulness and mercy
which Thou hast shown to Thy servant!" He will rather
take the gift as though he merited it. Still more will such a
man be incapable of perceiving God's kindness in the midst of
adversity and sorrow. The awareness of God's kindness to us
implies that we ourselves are kind and generous in dis-
position.
